name: Seljuk Empire
summary: A Turkic Sunni empire that took over Iran and Iraq. Its victory at Manzikert in 1071 opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement and helped trigger the Crusades.

knownFor.label: Battle of Manzikert
knownFor.note: Victory over Byzantium that opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement.

knownFor.label: Caravanserais
knownFor.note: Fortified roadside inns along trade routes, especially in Anatolia.

knownFor.label: Muqarnas vaults
knownFor.note: Honeycomb-like vaulting used in Seljuk mosques and madrasas.

knownFor.label: Nizamiyya madrasas
knownFor.note: A network of colleges founded by vizier Nizam al-Mulk.

location.value: Iran, Iraq, Central Asia and Anatolia, from the Hindu Kush to the Mediterranean at its height.
location.source: Wikipedia: Seljuk Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Peacock, The Great Seljuk Empire (2015)

terrain.value: The Iranian plateau, mountains and the Mesopotamian river plains.

climate.value: Arid, with good pastures for Turkmen herds in some regions.

resources.value: Farmland in oases and river valleys, pasture for Turkmen herds, and caravan trade.

urbanisation.value: Capitals at Nishapur, Ray and Isfahan; Isfahan grew into a great city.
urbanisation.source: Wikipedia: Seljuk Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Peacock, The Great Seljuk Empire (2015)

migration.value: Oghuz Turks moved into Iran and Anatolia.

economicBase.value: Farming, Turkmen herding and long-distance trade.

tradeRoutes.value: Silk Road routes protected by roadside inns (caravanserais).

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.

moneyAndTax.value: Gold and silver coins; the iqta‘ system gave officers the revenue of lands.

inequality.value: A Turkish military elite held land grants; Persian officials ran the state.

governmentType.value: A hereditary sultanate, nominally serving the Abbasid caliph.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Seljuk Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Peacock, The Great Seljuk Empire (2015)

keyRulers.value: Tughril (1037–1063), Alp Arslan, Malik-Shah I, Sanjar.

succession.value: Treated as family property, so lands were shared among relatives; this led to splits.

institutions.value: Vizier Nizam al-Mulk built a Persian-style bureaucracy and the Nizamiyya madrasas.

eliteConflict.value: Rival princes and powerful atabegs (guardians) fought for control.

armyAndTech.value: Turkmen horse archers plus a professional slave-soldier (ghulam) corps.

majorWars.value: Battle of Dandanaqan (1040), Manzikert (1071), the First Crusade, Qatwan (1141).
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Seljuk Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Peacock, The Great Seljuk Empire (2015)

territoryChange.value: About 3.9 million km² around 1080, from Anatolia to Central Asia.
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Seljuk Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Peacock, The Great Seljuk Empire (2015)

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Byzantium, the Fatimids and the Crusaders.

inventions.value: The Jalali calendar (1079), produced with Omar Khayyam.

scienceEducation.value: Nizamiyya madrasas; Omar Khayyam helped create the Jalali calendar (1079).

openness.source: Wikipedia: Seljuk Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Peacock, The Great Seljuk Empire (2015)

communicationTransport.value: Caravanserais (roadside inns) every day’s journey along trade roads, especially in Anatolia.

religion.value: Sunni Islam (Hanafi), with strong support for Sunni learning.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Seljuk Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Peacock, The Great Seljuk Empire (2015)

languageWriting.value: Persian for government and literature; Turkic for the army; Arabic for religion.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Seljuk Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Peacock, The Great Seljuk Empire (2015)

artsArchitecture.value: The four-iwan mosque plan and muqarnas vaults (e.g. the Great Mosque of Isfahan).

socialStructure.value: Turkish soldiers, Persian bureaucrats, merchants and peasants.

sharedIdentity.value: Sunni Islam and loyalty to the Seljuk family.

dailyLife.value: Mud-brick houses; bread, yoghurt, rice and meat; nomads in tents.

neighbours.value: Byzantium, the Fatimids, Georgia and the Khwarazmians.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Sunni madrasa education across the Middle East.

colonisation.value: None overseas; Turkic groups settled in Anatolia after the Battle of Manzikert (1071).

riseSignals.value: Victory over the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan (1040) and entry into Baghdad (1055).
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Seljuk Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Peacock, The Great Seljuk Empire (2015)

peakPeriod.value: Under Alp Arslan and Malik-Shah I (1063–1092), with vizier Nizam al-Mulk.

declineSignals.value: Succession wars after 1092, the Crusades, and defeat by the Qara Khitai at Qatwan (1141).
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Seljuk Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Peacock, The Great Seljuk Empire (2015)

outcome.value: The empire was replaced by the Khwarazmian Empire (1194) and the Zengids and Ayyubids; the Sultanate of Rum survived until 1308.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Seljuk Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Peacock, The Great Seljuk Empire (2015)

overallCertainty.value: Good for major events; casualty figures in chronicles are often exaggerated.
